en.text: This is Amluk-Dara Stupa, a large dome-shaped Buddhist stupa south of the Swat River. It is among the best-preserved in the valley, with a squarish plinth under a hemispherical dome visible for miles. The dome is 21 metres across and 7 metres tall. It is believed to have been built in the 3rd century CE. Aurel Stein found it in 1926. Domenico Faccenna studied it in the 1960s and 70s. It is unprotected and damaged by treasure hunters. Access is by road on the south side of the river near Barikot and Shamozai, then a short walk.

Bahrain is a riverside town at the confluence of the Daral and Swat rivers. Its name means two rivers, for that confluence. It has handicraft markets and is the trailhead and base camp for the Daral and Saidgai lakes trail. It lies 60 kilometres north of Mingora, with a year-round road.

Barikot is a town and gateway to central Swat. It is a base for the Bazira, Gumbat, Shingardar and Amluk-Dara sites. It lies on the middle course of the Swat River, about 20 kilometres from Mingora. Access is by the N-95 from Chakdara and Mingora.

Barikot Ghundai is the excavated ancient city on Barikot hill, identified with the Bazira stormed by Alexander in 327 BCE. Italian excavations since 1984 show occupation from the Bronze Age, a fortified city from the mid-first millennium BCE, an Indo-Greek wall and later Kushan and Buddhist phases. First traces of human presence are pit remains from around 1700 to 1400 BCE. An early-historic fortified town appears around 600 BCE. In 327 BCE Alexander the Great takes Bazira. Since 1984 the Italian Archaeological Mission has excavated here. Barikot is about 20 kilometres southwest of Mingora on the main road, and the hill site is reachable on foot from the road.

Butkara I Stupa is the largest excavated Buddhist stupa of the Swat plain, on the eastern edge of Mingora near Saidu Sharif. A core stupa of the Mauryan or early Indo-Greek period was encased five times and ringed by hundreds of votive stupas. It was probably built in the 2nd century BCE, with a possible Ashokan origin. A coin of Chandragupta Maurya in the oldest core layer supports an early date. Each enlargement was built over the previous structure. From 1956, the Italian Archaeological Mission led by Domenico Faccenna excavated the site. These excavations recovered much of the Gandharan sculpture now in the Swat Museum. The stupa is about 1 kilometre east of the Swat Museum, reachable by road year-round, flat, no hike.

Butkara III Stupa is a minor stupa site: a smaller Buddhist stupa with votive stupas. Excavated in the same Italian programme as Butkara I, it lies 1 kilometre south-east of it, on the Mingora outskirts. Short road access, no hike.

Chakdara Fort is a British-built hill fort commanding the Swat River crossing at the south entrance to Swat, on the site of an older Mughal fort and famed for its defence in 1897. In 1586 the Mughals built a fort at Chakdara. Between 1895 and 1896 the British occupied the site and built the present fort. In 1897 it was besieged during the Siege of Malakand. Chakdara lies on the road from Malakand to Swat. The fort is a military site, with a view from outside.

Daral Lake is an amoeba-shaped glacial lake above Bahrain. A shepherds' mosque stands near its shore. It sits at 3,505 metres and is accessible only in summer. Access is a 4 to 5 hour trek from Gabin Jabba or a 3 to 4 hour trek from Bahrain.

Elum Ghar, also Mount Ilam, is the prominent pyramid-like mountain on the Swat and Buner border south of Mingora. It is the highest peak in the region at 2,800 metres. It was a significant Hindu pilgrimage site, known as Ram Takht, until 1947. The mountain is the backdrop to Marghazar. Access is by a 1-day trek from the Marghazar or Pir Baba side. A local guide is advised.
Fatehpur is a union council and small town in Upper Swat, between Madyan and Khwazakhela. Access is via the main Swat valley road north of Mingora.
This is the Ghalegay Buddha, a rock carving. A Buddha figure is carved in rock beside the main road near Ghalegay, with cave remains alongside. It is roadside on the Mingora-Barikot road.
The Gogdara Rock Carvings are prehistoric and early-historic rock engravings in the Gogdara valley near Udegram. A local guide is helpful.

Gumbat Stupa, or Balo Kale, is a well-preserved Buddhist stupa in the Kandak valley west of Barikot, listed in Wikidata as Gumbat Stupa. Access is west of Barikot along the Kandak valley road, then a short walk.

A colossal seated Buddha relief is carved in a rock face in the Jahanabad side valley of Manglawar. Its style is compared to 7th-8th century Tang sculpture, and stylistic dating places the carving then. In 2007 an attack with explosives damaged the head. Italian conservators later restored it. Access is about 7 kilometres up the Malam Jabba road from Manglawar, with steps up to the rock.
Kanju is a village on the Swat River just north of Mingora. Saidu Sharif lies beside it. It is 3 kilometres from Mingora. Its peaches are widely known. It is reached on the Mingora-Kalam road.

Khwazakhela is a town in Swat, the second-largest commercial centre after Mingora. Shoppers from Kalam, Kohistan and Shangla come here to trade. It is a junction town for the Shangla road. It sits on the N 95 between Mingora and Madyan, with an all-year road.

Madyan is a bustling riverside town where the Chail and Swat valleys join. It is primarily inhabited by Torwalis. It serves as a dining and shopping stop and a base for the Bahrain-Kalam road. Access is on the N-95, about 55 kilometres from Mingora.

This is the excavated ruin of one of the earliest datable mosques in northern Pakistan. It has a rectangular hypostyle prayer hall with stone column bases, 28 metres by 21 metres. An Arabic inscription records a mosque founded in 1048 to 49 CE by the Ghaznavid general Amir Nustagin. The foundation inscription was found in 1984. Italian excavation ran from 1985 to 1999. Udegram is on the lower slope below Raja Gira Castle, a short walk from the village road.

Manglawar, also Manglor, is a town at the mouth of the Malam Jabba road. It was a former capital of the Kingdom of Swat. Buddhist reliefs and a stupa stand in its side valleys. It is 12 kilometres from Saidu Sharif, at the junction for Malam Jabba and Jahanabad.

Miandam is a forested hill-station valley west of the Swat River, at the foot of the Hindu Kush. It lies about 55 kilometres from Mingora. A WWF project here promotes sustainable harvesting of medicinal plants. A paved road reaches it from the Madyan or Mingora side. The season runs spring to autumn, with snow in winter.

Mingora is on the Swat River, the largest city of Swat and Malakand Division and the district capital. It is the base for the Butkara and Saidu Sharif Buddhist sites and the gateway to Fizagat, Malam Jabba, Madyan and Kalam. Main road hub. Swat Expressway from Chakdara, about 40 kilometres.
Nimogram Stupa is a Buddhist stupa on the western side of lower Swat. It lies west of Chakdara and Barikot, reached by local road.

Raja Gira Castle is a ruined hilltop fortification above Udegram, also called Odigram. Local tradition ties it to the Hindu ruler Raja Gira, attacked by Mahmud of Ghazni in the 11th century. A Ghaznavid-era mosque lies on its lower slope. In 1984 an Arabic inscription was found on the slope below the castle. Udegram is about 8 kilometres northwest of Mingora, and the climb is steep on foot.

This is the Saidu Sharif I Stupa and Monastery, a two-terrace Buddhist sacred area on the hillside above Saidu Sharif. The lower terrace holds a main stupa with minor stupas and viharas; a monastery stands above. The Italian Archaeological Mission excavated it, and it is a key site for early Gandharan art of Swat. The first building period ran from 25 BCE to the end of the 1st century, with a symmetrical layout. Excavation ran from 1963 to 1982, with a pause from 1966 to 1977. The site is at the edge of Saidu Sharif town, a short walk from the road, and is accessible year-round.

Saidu Sharif is a town and former capital quarter of the princely state of Swat, adjoining Mingora. It is named for Saidu Baba, the Akhund of Swat. Its older name was Baligram; in 1835 it was renamed Saidu Sharif. State-era royal buildings, Jahanzeb College and the Swat Museum cluster here. It is contiguous with Mingora.

The Shingardar Stupa is a large Buddhist stupa of slate and stone near Ghalegay, between Mingora and Barikot. Tradition links it to King Uttarasena's share of the Buddha's relics, and says he built it to enshrine them. In the British period it was identified by Deane and Aurel Stein. It is just off the main road between Ghalegay and Barikot.

The Swat Museum is the archaeological museum of Swat, on the Mingora-Saidu Sharif road. It holds Gandharan sculpture, reliquaries and an ethnographic gallery. Most holdings come from Butkara I and Odigram. The museum was conceived in 1959 by the Italian Archaeological Mission and the Wali of Swat. In 2005 the Kashmir earthquake badly damaged it. In 2007 and 2008 it closed during the conflict, and its contents moved to Taxila. A bomb exploded nearby in February 2008 and damaged the building. In July 2011, 2,700 objects returned. A new seismic-resistant museum opened on 11 December 2014. Opening days can be checked locally.

Udegram, also called Odigram, is a village on the Swat River northwest of Mingora. It is identified with ancient Ora of Alexander's campaign. It hosts the Raja Gira castle and a Ghaznavid-era mosque. In 327 BCE Alexander stormed Odigram. From the 8th century the Hindu Shahi dynasty had its capital at Udigram. Access is 8 kilometres northwest of Mingora by road.

The White Palace at Marghazar is the white marble summer palace of Swat's first ruler, Miangul Abdul Wadud. It is now a hotel, set among large chinar trees below Elum Ghar, including a 200-year-old chinar tree. In 1935 Wadud decided to build a summer residence. The palace was built and completed between 1940 and 1941. Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip stayed three days in 1961. The palace is 13 kilometres from Saidu Sharif on a paved hill road. It is open year-round, cool in summer, and has day visits.
